title: Proof
full_review:
The certainties of life are far from the incontrovertible ones you might find in a math equation, as you discover in "Proof" (Miramax), the absorbing adaptation of David Auburn's Tony- and Pulitzer Prize-winning Broadway play.

The Chicago-based story concerns a 27-year-old woman named Catherine (Gwyneth Paltrow) who is coping with the mental illness -- and subsequent death -- of her genius mathematician father, Robert (Anthony Hopkins).

Just as she has inherited her father's proficiency in math, she fears she also inherited his madness, worrying she'll go "bughouse" as he did.

She had to cut short her studies at Northwestern to return home and take care of him after his apparent remission from schizophrenia proved short-lived. Against all advice, she refused to institutionalize him, and let him stay home among the things he loved.

The film begins as preparations for the father's funeral are under way, though Robert -- in the larger-than-life persona of Hopkins -- shows up in flashbacks and in dialogue with Catherine. Her sister, Claire (Hope Davis, looking uncannily like Hillary Rodham Clinton here), a controlling perfectionist notably absent during their father's long illness, arrives from New York, with every intention of taking her disturbed sister back with her.

Hal (Jake Gyllenhaal) is a frequent visitor to the house. He's a math geek who was Robert's former student and is now a math teacher at the University of Chicago, and plays in a rock band on the side. He hopes, in going through Robert's numerous notebooks, that he'll find some amazing mathematical revelation.

Claire's compulsively meticulous ways -- such as making endless lists -- are a total irritant to Catherine. After the funeral, Catherine succumbs to Hal's gentle admission of love. He reveals he has long had a crush on her, and they have a sexual encounter (brief, and no nudity).

Midway through the film, a startling twist turns the plot trajectory on its ear.

Working from the script by Auburn and Rebecca Miller, director John Madden has sensibly opened up the play from the stage without debasing the original, and there are strong performances by the leads, especially Paltrow, who portrayed Catherine in a London run, where she was, in fact, directed by Madden. She cannily pulls you in and makes you empathize utterly with her troubled and fragile demeanor.

The play's theme of trying to grab hold of "proofs" in life when they don't always exist resonates as well as ever. Clearly, some things -- like love and trust (and, we can add, faith) -- can never be "proven" in a mathematical or scientific sense and must be verified in less concrete terms.

Despite having mathematics as its central topic, numbers are secondary to a very human story, and that's what really counts.

The film contains scattered instances of profanity, rough and crude language and
expressions, a nongraphic premarital sexual encounter, other brief sexual references, and drug use, making this best for older adolescents and up. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
